name: Iris Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a scraper at a large mine and start by walking round the belt housing and checking the guards. I came into this particular machine late, so I ask an experienced operator before cutting into ground that has shifted after rain. The pay is good and I like the crew, though I dislike being hurried when a load target looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the machine still needs a person to hear a strange rattle and stop before a belt is damaged. I would also tell the women on my shift that the mine should not use a small software update to quietly change our break times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quieter picture suits me, though I'm not entirely comfortable as the newest scraper operator. I earn good money here and we have about ten months of bills saved, but I still have to ask an older hand about the edge of the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep operating the scraper and checking the belt before each shift. I'll take our roster to the union meeting next month and ask whether the break times changed; if nothing shifts during the first year, I'll stay on the same job and keep our savings intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly at ease because I know where my next wage is coming from. The machine is loud enough already without a new worry added to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the shift still catches you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cut looks different after rain, and I sometimes take an extra minute to judge it. An experienced operator named Priya has shown me how to keep the scraper from biting too deep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner say about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jo wants us to keep a good reserve for when I stop work. Our grown children have their own homes, so we are thinking about our own bills and the occasional visit, not school fees.

say: I would say the **scraper** still needs an operator who hears mechanical trouble.
I would tell my shift that even small software changes need **fair breaks**.
think: I am still **learning the cut**, despite earning good wages.
Our **ten-month reserve** gives us room, though retirement is near.
do: Continue paid **scraper shifts** and check the belt housing before every morning run.
Take the **roster** to next month’s union meeting.
feel: Mostly at ease about **wages**, with ordinary work still demanding care.
S0.quote: The machine is loud enough already without a new worry added to it.
fieldNote: She has strong savings and good wages, so her **ordinary work** feels secure despite being a junior operator.
Her union concern concerns **break times**, a modest but specific workplace change she would verify from the roster.

steps.text: Keep operating the scraper and checking the belt before shifts
Take the shift roster to the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the planning office may change faster than the pit, and we should not let the office workers stand alone. I would ask the union to make the mine show where software decisions come from when shifts or loads change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried a program could set a pace that feels fine on a screen and rough on the ground. I do not use AI myself, and I would want a person I trust to explain any new instruction before I move this machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my scraper shifts and write down each load target beside the actual ground conditions. In the first year I'll bring those notes to the safety representative and join a meeting about any new planning system; I won't press a button I don't understand during a live run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary rather than frightened for my own job right away. I feel more concern for the planners who could lose hours and for the drivers asked to meet impossible targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in those notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the target, the time, and whether the ground was wet or broken. I already keep a pocket book for fuel checks, so another page is easier for me than a new phone app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you refuse a new system altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd try it on a stopped machine with a person explaining it. I don't trust being rushed into a live shift and then blamed for a bad instruction.

say: I would say **planners** deserve support when thinking tasks move to software.
I would ask the union to demand clear reasons for **software-set targets**.
think: I fear a screen may set an unsafe **work pace**.
I need a trusted person to explain instructions because I **never use AI** myself.
do: Continue paid **scraper work** during the first year.
Record **load targets** and ground conditions in my pocket book.
Bring the notes to a **safety meeting** about the new system.
feel: Wary for myself and concerned for **office staff** and drivers.
S1.quote: I don't trust being rushed into a live shift and then blamed for a bad instruction.
fieldNote: She does not reject all technology, but insists on a **stopped-machine explanation** before accepting new instructions.
Her concern reaches beyond her own wages to **planners and drivers**, consistent with her union involvement.

steps.text: Keep working paid scraper shifts as planning software spreads
Bring recorded load targets and ground conditions to the union safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would put the office in danger first, then capable robots around 2031 could take the scraper. I would ask the union to bargain for a paid route out before the mine decides who is surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 I might still be operating, but at 63 the hands-on work could disappear. We have ten months of bills saved, which gives us time to choose, yet it would be foolish to call that enough to retire without checking our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll get the union's help requesting a written redeployment plan and a funded safety-inspection course. I'll enroll only if the mine pays and keeps my wages during training; after 2028 I'll work the scraper while it is staffed and apply to a nearby mine if our shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the speed, even with savings behind us. My fear is being told I'm too old to train while the robot gets a brand-new manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why safety inspection rather than another machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already inspect the belt and stop work when I see a fault, so the duties make sense to me. I would still need proper instruction and a real vacancy, and I won't pretend a short course guarantees either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Jo about the two dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jo that office work might turn in 2028 and my machine around 2031. We would keep the savings for bills while I push for paid training, not spend it as if retirement has arrived.

say: I would say **office roles** face 2028 before robots threaten operators around 2031.
I would ask the union for **paid redeployment** before cuts are announced.
think: At **63**, I could lose hands-on scraper work to capable robots.
Our **ten-month reserve** gives time to decide, but cannot prove retirement is affordable.
do: Request a **written redeployment plan** through the union this month.
Enroll in **safety-inspection training** only if funded with wages.
Apply to a **nearby mine** if scraper shifts fall.
feel: Alarmed by the **speed**, despite a useful savings cushion.
S2.quote: My fear is being told I'm too old to train while the robot gets a brand-new manual.
fieldNote: She uses the savings cushion for **decision time**, while refusing to assume an affordable retirement at 63.
Her proposed training needs **funding and wages**; the nearby mine application depends on actual lost shifts.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written mine redeployment plan
Enroll in safety-inspection training if funded with continued wages
Keep operating the scraper after 2028 while shifts remain
Apply at a nearby mine if scraper shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that five years gives us time to negotiate while there are still people doing the work. The office would meet thinking AI around 2031, and the scraper crew could meet capable robots around 2034; I would want each date written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 at the first date and 66 at the second. I might be ready to stop full shifts by 66, but I need a real retirement estimate rather than an age scribbled on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the pension office for a written estimate this year, and Jo and I will list what the house costs each month. I'll carry on in the scraper cab, and after 2031 I'll use union meetings to press for paid training places before the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but the five years let me count and argue instead of simply reacting. I still don't enjoy the thought of becoming a spare person beside a working machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see in the estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the monthly amount and what happens if I stop at 66 instead of later. My partner Jo has income too, but we should put both numbers against the bills rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train even if you could retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the numbers covered our life, I might choose fewer shifts and leave a training place to someone younger. If they did not, I would ask for paid instruction rather than take an unpaid gamble.

say: I would ask our union branch for both **2031 and 2034** dates in writing.
I would press for **paid training places** while crews still work.
think: I might stop full shifts at **66**, depending on actual retirement income.
I refuse to treat an **age on a calendar** as a financial plan.
do: Request a written **retirement estimate** this year.
Continue paid **scraper shifts** through the warning years.
Attend union meetings to secure **funded training** before 2034.
feel: Uneasy, but able to **count and negotiate** with five years.
S3.quote: I need a real retirement estimate rather than an age scribbled on the calendar.
fieldNote: She separates a possible retirement at **66** from a guaranteed income and insists on written figures.
The longer runway supports **union bargaining** while the mine still needs people in its cabs.

steps.text: Continue paid scraper shifts while operators are needed
Attend union meetings to press for paid training places before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine has a decade to work out fair exits and proper training, not just a last-minute farewell. Thinking AI in 2036 would hit office work first, and capable robots around 2039 could take the machine work if I were still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 when the office changes and 71 when robots can operate. I expect to have stopped regular scraper shifts by then if Jo and I can make the numbers work, but I do not want anyone younger to face an empty promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on paid shifts while I can and ask the pension office for a written estimate now. If our income covers the bills, I'll plan a gradual reduction before 2039; meanwhile I'll bring a proposal to the union to use experienced operators as paid trainers for the next crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer about my own wage in this long picture. I still feel angry at the idea of a whole crew being thanked and dismissed without a handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why paid trainers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An operator knows when the rock feels wrong under a machine, and the next crew needs that lesson before the mine changes equipment. I would help teach if the position were real and paid, not a volunteer speech at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your retirement estimate falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep taking paid shifts while I am fit and check openings at other nearby mines. I would not ask my grown children to finance a gap just because I guessed at a pension.

say: I would say a decade permits **fair exits** and useful training.
I would ask the mine to pay experienced operators as **trainers**.
think: At **71**, I hope to be off regular scraper shifts if household numbers allow.
I worry younger crews may receive only an **empty promise**.
do: Continue **paid shifts** while fit and needed.
Get a written **retirement estimate** before reducing work.
Take a **paid-trainer proposal** to the union.
feel: Calmer for my own income, but angry about **unfair dismissal**.
S4.quote: I would not ask my grown children to finance a gap just because I guessed at a pension.
fieldNote: Her personal exposure is lower at the **2039 robot date**, yet she keeps a strong concern for younger crews.
Even a gradual exit depends on **verified income**; her trainer idea would require a real paid role.

steps.text: Keep taking paid scraper shifts while fit and needed
Take the paid operator-trainer proposal to the union branch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable robots could take my scraper work around 2031 when I am 63. A written redeployment plan, paid safety-inspection training and union bargaining before the cuts would help me use our savings to choose sensibly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets to check the robot's safety claims. I'd want operators and safety representatives involved, because a clean company brochure cannot show you what wet ground does to a machine.

headlineQuote: I'd want operators and safety representatives involved, because a clean company brochure cannot show you what wet ground does to a machine.
portrait: Iris is a **58-year-old junior** scraper operator who earns well but still asks colleagues about unfamiliar ground.
She and her partner have roughly **ten months** of expenses saved; their grown children support themselves.
She avoids **AI tools** and seeks human explanations before accepting new instructions during a live shift.
Her union work focuses on **safe targets**, paid training and a fair exit from machine work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her only until around 2031 before robots could take her scraper shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written redeployment plan**, funded safety-inspection training and early union bargaining would let her plan.
